gdp_growth.label: Real GDP growth, calendar year
gdp_growth.note: Chained volume measure, percentage change on the previous calendar year. Full calendar years only; 2025 is the latest complete year. Latest years are open to revision.

gdp_quarterly.label: Real GDP growth, quarter on previous quarter
gdp_quarterly.note: Chained volume measure, seasonally adjusted, percentage change on the previous quarter. The latest quarter is a first estimate.

productivity_oph.label: Output per hour worked, whole economy
productivity_oph.note: Index, 2023 = 100, quarterly, seasonally adjusted. Output per hour is derived partly from LFS hours worked, so it carries the LFS quality caveat.

employment_rate.label: Employment rate, aged 16 to 64
employment_rate.note: Three-month average, seasonally adjusted. LFS estimate: the ONS advises caution with short-term changes (see notes). Points are placed at the middle month of each three-month period.

unemployment_rate.label: Unemployment rate, aged 16 and over
unemployment_rate.note: Three-month average, seasonally adjusted. LFS estimate: the ONS advises caution with short-term changes (see notes). Points are placed at the middle month of each three-month period.

pay_growth.label: Regular pay growth, whole economy
pay_growth.note: Average weekly earnings, regular pay (excluding bonuses and arrears), three-month average on the same period a year earlier, seasonally adjusted, nominal (not adjusted for inflation). From the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey of employers, not the LFS. Points are placed at the middle month of each three-month period.

labour_share.label: Compensation of employees as a share of GDP
labour_share.note: Computed here as 100 x DTWM / YBHA (both current prices, annual; YBHA from source ons_ybha), rounded to one decimal place. Annual series; 2025 is the latest full calendar year (the quarterly accounts cover only part of the current year). Excludes the labour income of the self-employed (mixed income), so it is lower than labour-share measures that adjust for self-employment.

obr_gdp_forecast.label: OBR forecast of real GDP growth
obr_gdp_forecast.note: The OBR's central forecast, October 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook (presented 28 October 2026, corrected 30 October 2026). All years shown are forecasts, not outturns. The same table gives 1.3% as the OBR's 2025 outturn; the later ONS estimate (IHYP) differs, so the two are not spliced.

business_ai_use.label: Businesses using at least one AI technology, all sizes
business_ai_use.note: Business Insights and Conditions Survey, private-sector businesses in the industries BICS covers (it excludes, among others, agriculture, finance and insurance, and public administration), weighted by count of businesses. Survey question: "Which of the following artificial intelligence technologies, if any, does your business currently use?" Options: Autonomous vehicles; Data processing using machine learning; Image processing using machine learning; Robotics; Text generation using Large Language Models; Visual content creation; Other (Please describe); Not sure; Business does not currently use artificial intelligence technologies. Dates are the midpoint of each wave.

workers_high_exposure_high_complementari.label: Workers in occupations with high AI exposure and high complementarity
workers_high_exposure_high_complementari.note: IMF estimates as reported by DSIT/AISI. DSIT: the IMF measures exposure using an index of the correspondence between AI applications and the human abilities each occupation requires; its complementarity assessment is based on the social and physical context of work, and in high-complementarity roles AI may be more likely to boost efficiency and productivity. DSIT notes such indices are indicative rather than precise. The two high-exposure groups sum to 67%; the DSIT text says 'around 70%'.

notes: Official published data only; no PolicyEngine modelling. The OBR series is the OBR's own forecast.

Labour Force Survey quality: in its labour market bulletin released 2026-10-20 (https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/uklabourmarket/october2026) the ONS says LFS response has improved and is now close to its pre-pandemic level, but that some volatility remains, particularly in estimates for mid-2023 and throughout 2024 and in detailed breakdowns with small samples, and advises users to focus on long-term movements rather than short-term changes. LFS estimates are official statistics; the ONS has told the Office for Statistics Regulation it will not seek reaccreditation for them and is prioritising the Transformed LFS as their replacement.
LFS rolling three-month estimates are labelled in ONS files by their middle month, and AWE three-month averages by their last month; periods here are given as the full three months.
GDP and productivity figures are revised as new data arrive; values are as published on the release dates in 'sources'.
The OBR October 2026 EFO gives 2025 GDP growth of 1.3% (its outturn at the time); the ONS series IHYP gives 1.2%. The difference is a data vintage, not a forecast.

Calendar-year series (GDP growth, compensation of employees as a share of GDP) end at the latest full year; the current year appears only in the quarterly and monthly series, labelled by its quarters or months.
Compensation of employees as a share of GDP is the only computed series (a ratio of two ONS series); it is not the ONS's self-employment-adjusted labour share.

Exposure by SOC major group is null: the DfE report 'The impact of AI on UK jobs and training' (November 2023) publishes AIOE scores only for 4-digit SOC 2010 unit groups with no major-group table or employment counts, and no later DfE/DSIT source with SOC 2020 major-group scores was found. Aggregating the unit-group scores ourselves (for example an unweighted mean by major group) is possible but would be our own construction on SOC 2010.
BICS covers private-sector businesses in selected industries; results for businesses with 0 to 9 employees carry large survey weights, so the ONS often headlines the 10-or-more-employees figure.
